name: ABP 692
summary: ABP 692 is Amgen's own proposed biosimilar to Ocrevus (ocrelizumab), an anti-CD20 antibody infused twice a year. The Phase 3 is NCT06700343: a randomised, double-blind PK/PD similarity study against US and EU Ocrevus in 152 patients with relapsing-remitting MS. Its primary endpoint is AUC to day 15, and primary completion is estimated for 2027-04-19. Price anchor: Ocrevus at $56,845 per CMS Part B beneficiary in 2024, times 0.520, which is what Medicare paid per 10 mg unit of Amgen's Riabni against Rituxan in 2024. That gives $29,557 a year, or $25,266 net once the biosimilar add-on is taken off. Uptake anchor: rituximab biosimilars took 60% of Medicare Part B rituximab claims in 2022 (Qian, AJMC 2024). Amgen is given a third of that class share, one of three developers with a comparative trial running. The reach is the ocrelizumab-treated 9.2% of the book's 913,925 MS pool. US launch follows the 12-year BPCIA exclusivity ending 2029-03-28 (Ocrevus first licensed 2017-03-28; the book's Purple Book row is that computed statutory floor, and BR&R 2025-10-21 puts exclusivity through March 2029), so 2030 is the first full year.

therapy_mode.source: Ocrevus label dosing (BLA 761053, first licensed 2017-03-28; book approvals row from openFDA): 600 mg IV every 6 months after a split first dose. The book's frexalimab price row notes that Ocrevus maintenance is two infusions a year. A biosimilar carries the reference's dosing
therapy_mode.check: Value 'chronic' unchanged. Source corrected: the researcher cited Ocrevus as BLA 125877, but the book's approvals table (openFDA) holds Ocrevus, asset 563, as BLA761053 approved 2017-03-28 (Ocrevus Zunovo is BLA761371). The frexalimab seed note (data/assumptions/sny_frexalimab.csv) does say maintenance is two infusions a year and beneficiaries take 1.78 (20,976 claims / 11,764 = 1.78, CMS Part B 2024). The label's 600 mg every 6 months was not re-read here (Amass regulatorycore out of quota, DailyMed text not stored in the book); it is the standard label and consistent with the two-a-year note.

list_price_per_patient.source: Two book rows. (1) lookup.py demand Ocrevus: CMS Part B 2024, $668,719,044 over 11,764 beneficiaries = $56,845 per beneficiary, the figure the book's frexalimab seed also uses. (2) The per-unit price discount of Amgen's own marketed anti-CD20 biosimilar (lookup.py demand Riabni / Rituxan). In CMS Part B 2024, Riabni (Q5123, 10 mg units) was $92,447,260 over 2,331,225 units = $39.656 per unit. Rituxan (J9312, 10 mg units) was $436,980,635 over 5,729,505 units = $76.268. The ratio is 0.5200. $56,845 x 0.5200 = $29,557
list_price_per_patient.note: Judgement on the discount comparator and year. Riabni is the closest analogue in the book. It is Amgen's own biosimilar, and like ABP 692 it copies an infused anti-CD20 antibody paid under Part B. The seeds suggested for Pavblu, Wezlana and Bkemv are empty in this book, and none of the three has a Part B row in drug_demand. 2024 is Riabni's fourth full year. Its ratio to Rituxan fell from 0.899 (2021) to 0.655 (2022), 0.561 (2023) and 0.520 (2024), so a flat price at the year-4 level understates the early years. It overstates the late years: Ruxience, the first-wave rituximab biosimilar, was down to 0.264 of Rituxan per unit by 2024. The same test on Amgen's other Part B biosimilars in 2024, per 10 mg unit, gives a range. Avsola against J1745 infliximab is 0.730. Mvasi against Avastin is 0.36, but Avastin's Part B units include intravitreal eye use, so that ratio is not clean. Kanjinti against Herceptin is 0.23. Published erosion points the same way. Qian (AJMC 2024, PMID 39745502) finds the rituximab biosimilars' Part B spending per dosage unit fell 15% to 26% in 2022 alone. Kim et al. (JCO Oncol Pract 2026, PMID 42413074) put bevacizumab biosimilars 52.2% below the originator per administration by 2023. The Ocrevus per-beneficiary figure is 89% of a full patient-year (its beneficiaries take 1.78 infusions against a maintenance two). This follows the house per-beneficiary convention; the frexalimab seed makes the same point
list_price_per_patient.check: lookup.py demand, CMS Part B 2024: Ocrevus $668,719,044.2 / 11,764 = $56,844.53; Riabni $92,447,259.69 / 2,331,225 units = $39.656; Rituxan $436,980,635.1 / 5,729,504.8 units = $76.268; ratio 0.51995. $56,844.53 x 0.51995 = $29,556.5 = 0.029557 mm. Units consistent: Riabni 272 and Rituxan 257 units per beneficiary, so both are 10 mg units. Year path recomputed: 0.899 (2021), 0.655, 0.561, 0.520; Ruxience 2024 $20.148/unit = 0.264 of Rituxan. Side ratios: Avsola/Infliximab* 0.730, Mvasi/Avastin 0.362, Kanjinti/Herceptin 0.233, all match. Pavblu, Wezlana, Bkemv have no drug_demand rows and no seeds (lookup.py seed empty). PubMed: Qian AJMC 2024 (PMID 39745502) abstract says biosimilar ASPDU fell 15% to 26% in 2022 in Medicare Part B and Medicaid; Kim JCO OP 2026 (PMID 42413074) per-administration savings 52.2% by 2023. A departure from the house anchor (Ocrevus at 1.0), labelled a judgement with the case both ways; a biosimilar priced at the reference would be the less defensible read.

gross_to_net_pct.source: SSA section 1847A(b)(8), as amended by IRA section 11403 (CMS, 'Frequently Asked Questions: Inflation Reduction Act', cms.gov/files/document/biosimilar-faqs.pdf). Medicare pays a qualifying biosimilar its own ASP plus 8% of the REFERENCE product's ASP, not 6% of its own. So the Riabni-derived figure carries an add-on of 8% of Rituxan's ASP. Rituxan's ASP is $76.268 / 1.06 = $71.951 per unit, and 8% of it is $5.756. $5.756 / $39.656 = 0.1452 off the Part B figure
gross_to_net_pct.note: Judgement: this departs from the house 0.056604 for a Part B anchor, on the same principle (take the Part B figure back to ASP, which is already net of discounts). A biosimilar's add-on is set on the reference's ASP, and at about half the reference's price that add-on is a larger share of its own payment. Direction checked: 0.1452 off list, so net is $29,557 x 0.8548 = $25,266 per patient-year. That is 47.1% of Ocrevus's ASP of $53,627. The case against: the house 0.056604 would give a net of $27,884, 10% higher. The 8% add-on runs only for biosimilars first paid by 2027-12-31. A 2029 launch reverts to 6% of the reference ASP, which changes the Part B payment (the list) but not the ASP (the net)
gross_to_net_pct.check: Statute verified. CMS 'Frequently Asked Questions: Inflation Reduction Act' (cms.gov/files/document/biosimilar-faqs.pdf, via WebSearch) and the ASPE June 2023 brief: IRA section 11403 amends SSA 1847A(b)(8) so a qualifying biosimilar (ASP not above the reference's ASP) is paid its ASP plus 8% of the REFERENCE product's ASP, for 5 years from 2022-10-01 where ASP payment was already made by 2022-09-30, or from the quarter of first payment where that falls 2022-10-01 to 2027-12-31; otherwise the base rule is ASP plus 6% of the reference's ASP. Riabni was paid on ASP from 2021, so 2024 sits inside its 2022-10-01 to 2027-09-30 window, and its ASP is below Rituxan's, so the 8% applies. Arithmetic: Rituxan ASP 76.268/1.06 = 71.951; 8% = 5.756; 5.756/39.656 = 0.14515. Net = 29,556.5 x 0.85485 = $25,266; Ocrevus ASP 56,844.5/1.06 = 53,627; 25,266/53,627 = 0.4712, identical to Riabni ASP/Rituxan ASP (33.900/71.951), so the list and the off-list share are internally consistent. House 0.056604 would give $27,884 (10.4% higher) and would wrongly treat the add-on as 6% of the biosimilar's own ASP. Direction right (share off list). The note's point that a 2029 launch gets 6% of the reference ASP is correct and moves list, not net.

discontinuation_pct.unit: share of the treated stock stopping per year
discontinuation_pct.source: Pardo G et al., Neurology and Therapy 2022;11:337-351 (PMID 35020156, doi:10.1007/s40120-021-00319-3). IBM MarketScan Commercial and Medicare Supplemental, 524 ocrelizumab initiators: 75% persistent at 24 months (no switch and no gap of 60 days or more). 1 - 0.75^(1/2) = 0.134 a year
discontinuation_pct.note: The biosimilar's patients are ocrelizumab patients, so ocrelizumab's own persistence applies, not the 28.6% ofatumumab figure the frexalimab seed uses. The case for lower: Engmann et al., JMCP 2021 (PMID 33624535, doi:10.18553/jmcp.2021.20413) find 8% of ocrelizumab starters in PharMetrics Plus stop within 12 months and 17% within 18 months (11.7% a year). The case for higher: both studies are Genentech-funded. A biosimilar also loses some patients back to the reference: in oncology, 1.2% switched from a biosimilar to the reference within 12 months (Liu et al., JAMA Oncol 2026, PMID 42658505)
discontinuation_pct.check: PubMed PMID 35020156 (Pardo, Neurol Ther 2022;11:337-351, doi 10.1007/s40120-021-00319-3): MarketScan Commercial and Medicare Supplemental, OCR n = 524, persistence 75% at 24 months, persistence = no switch and no gap of 60 days or more; authors from Genentech. 1 - 0.75^0.5 = 0.1340. PMID 33624535 (Engmann, JMCP 2021): OCR 8% discontinued at 12 months, 17% at 18 months; 1 - 0.83^(12/18) = 0.117, matches the 11.7%. PMID 42658505 (Liu, JAMA Oncol 2026): 170 patients (1.2%) switched from biosimilar to reference within 12 months of initiation. All as stated.

forecast_start_year.source: 12-year BPCIA reference product exclusivity (PHS Act 351(k)(7)(A)): a biosimilar licence cannot take effect until 12 years after the reference's first licensure. Ocrevus (BLA 761053) was first licensed 2017-03-28 (book approvals row, openFDA), so 2029-03-28. The book's exclusivities row for asset 563 carries 2029-03-28 as a '12-year statutory floor' computed from the Purple Book licensure date (backend/fetchers/exclusivity_purplebook.py), not as a date the Purple Book publishes. BR&R, 'The Early Outlook for Ocrelizumab Biosimilars', 2025-10-21 (biosimilarsrr.com/2025/10/21/the-early-outlook-for-ocrelizumab-biosimilars/): exclusivity runs through March 2029 and the primary US patent expires after October 2028. NCT06700343 primary completion 2027-04-19, estimated (book trials table)
forecast_start_year.note: Judgement on timing. A PK/PD readout in 2027 leaves time to file and be approved before the exclusivity date, so launch is expected in 2029 and 2030 is the first full year. The curve starts in 2030, so any revenue from Q2 to Q4 2029 is left out. The case against: Ocrevus Zunovo (subcutaneous, approved 2024-09-13) carries 2036-09-13 in the book, which is again the computed 12-year floor from its licensure date and not an FDA exclusivity determination, so it may not hold; either way an IV biosimilar cannot substitute for it. Roche can move patients onto it before 2029, and an IV biosimilar cannot substitute for it. Roche's remaining patents are not checked here, and BPCIA litigation could delay entry
forecast_start_year.check: Value 2030 unchanged; source and note corrected. The book's row (exclusivities id 3328, asset 563, identifier '12-year statutory floor', source purple_book) is the fetcher's computed floor from the licensure date, used when the Purple Book publishes no reference-product exclusivity date; the researcher presented it as a Purple Book exclusivity date. The Purple Book itself and openFDA could not be opened (proxy 403); no SEC filing states the date (Amgen and Biogen 10-Ks searched in the book: Biogen says only 'approved in the U.S. in 2017' and that its Ocrevus royalty halves on first biosimilar entry). The date holds on the statute plus the 2017-03-28 licensure (book approvals row BLA761053) plus BR&R 2025-10-21, which WebSearch confirms states exclusivity through March 2029 and primary patent after October 2028. Book trials table: NCT06700343, Amgen, Phase 3, active not recruiting, 152 enrolled, primary completion 2027-04-19 (estimated), completion 2027-10-04, AUC0-d15 primary endpoint. Launch 2029 and 2030 as first full year is consistent.

exus_multiple.source: MVASI FY2025, Amgen 10-K 0000318154-26-000010 (book filing_sections, product sales table): ROW $198mm against US $573mm. 198 / 573 = 0.3455
exus_multiple.note: Judgement on the comparator. Mvasi is Amgen's longest-selling infused antibody biosimilar with a split it reports separately. Riabni, Avsola and Kanjinti are reported only inside 'Other'. The case for higher: Ocrevus's own FY2025 split is (CHF 1,451mm Europe + 685mm International) / 4,874mm US = 0.438 (Roche Finance Information Tool, sheet 'P Sales Regions CHF'), and Mvasi's 2023 to 2025 average is 765 / 1,533 = 0.499. The case for lower: Celltrion and Sandoz are stronger in European tenders, and Pavblu reads 0.013 (9 / 691)
exus_multiple.check: Book filing_sections, Amgen 10-K 0000318154-26-000010 (mdna, 'Other product sales by geographic region'): MVASI U.S. 573 / 449 / 511 and ROW 198 / 278 / 289 for 2025 / 2024 / 2023; PAVBLU U.S. 691, ROW 9. 198/573 = 0.3455; (289+278+198)/(511+449+573) = 765/1,533 = 0.499; 9/691 = 0.013. Roche workbook (backend/tests/fixtures/roche_group_financial_data.xlsx, sheet 'P Sales Regions CHF', 2025): Ocrevus 7,010 = US 4,874 + Europe 1,451 + Japan 0 + International 685; (1,451+685)/4,874 = 0.438. All as stated; labelled judgement.

economics_share.source: Amgen 10-K FY2025 (0000318154-26-000010) lists 'ABP 692 Investigational biosimilar to OCREVUS (ocrelizumab)' among its Phase 3 programmes and names no collaborator. The same pipeline section names partners elsewhere (TEZSPIRE with AstraZeneca). The Q2 2026 results release (8-K 0000318154-26-000124) reports the ABP 692 study has completed enrolment, again with no partner. Amgen is lead sponsor of NCT06700343
economics_share.check: Book filing_sections: Amgen 10-K 0000318154-26-000010 lists 'ABP 692 Investigational biosimilar to OCREVUS (ocrelizumab)' in Phase 3 with no collaborator, while naming AstraZeneca for TEZSPIRE and AMG 104. Q2 2026 8-K 0000318154-26-000124 exhibit: the ABP 692 PK similarity/comparative study 'has completed enrollment', no partner named. Book trials table: lead sponsor Amgen. 1.0 holds.

prevalence.source: carried by the book: data/epidemiology.csv 'Multiple Sclerosis', 913,925 US adults (Wallin MT et al., Neurology 2019). backend/epidemiology.py aliases 'Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting' to it
prevalence.note: Carried by the book. The count covers relapsing and progressive forms together. That matches a biosimilar, which by extrapolation takes every Ocrevus indication, PPMS included
prevalence.check: Null by design. lookup.py pool 'Multiple Sclerosis': epidemiology.csv carries 913,925 (Wallin, Neurology 2019); backend/epidemiology.py ALIASES maps 'Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting' to 'Multiple Sclerosis'. No seed on any MS indication states a prevalence, so no second figure exists.

incidence.source: the book's own MS convention: the frexalimab ('Multiple Sclerosis') and fenebrutinib ('Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive') seeds state 0.0 because no national US incidence sits beside Wallin's prevalence, and the epidemiology.csv row has none
incidence.note: Stated rather than null because a blank incidence leaves the engine's derived mode unavailable. This matches the other MS seeds, so it adds no second figure. Its effect: new ocrelizumab starts after launch are not in the pool, so the biosimilar's stock decays once the pool is drawn down. See penetration_peak_pct
incidence.check: lookup.py pool 'Multiple Sclerosis' and a direct read of book.db across all scenarios: the only MS incidence rows are Frexalimab on 'Multiple Sclerosis' 0.0 and Fenebrutinib on 'Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive' 0.0; no asset carries any incidence on 'Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting' (indication id 86); epidemiology.csv's MS incidence is blank. So 0.0 matches every other MS seed and no different figure exists to use. The guard test_no_two_assets_disagree_about_how_many_people_have_a_disease groups by indication_id, and 0.0 would pass it even if pooled across the three MS names. backend/forecast.py confirms the derived mode needs incidence non-null (line 137) and that the fill from the disease file is per figure, so a null would stay null here.

eligible_pct.source: The reference's own treated share. Ocrevus had 11,764 CMS Part B and 3,085 Part D beneficiaries in 2024 (lookup.py demand Ocrevus), 14,849 in all. That is against the 78,050 CMS 2024 disease-modifying-therapy beneficiaries the frexalimab seed sums across the Part B and D files, so 19.02%. Times the 48.49% of Medicare MS patients on any disease-modifying therapy (Li J, Hutton GJ, Aparasu RR, Multiple Sclerosis Journal 2025, as carried by the frexalimab seed): 9.225%. Applied to 913,925, that is 84,312 US patients on Ocrevus
eligible_pct.note: How the reference's treated share is applied: a biosimilar reaches only patients who would otherwise get ocrelizumab, so the pool is Ocrevus's patients, and penetration is the rate at which they move to ABP 692. Cross-check: Roche's FY2025 US Ocrevus sales of CHF 4,874mm (Roche Finance Information Tool) at USD 1.2152 per CHF is $5,923mm. Divided by a full-year ASP of $65,185 (1,200 mg at $54.32 per mg, from CMS Part B 2024 $668.7mm over 11.61mm 1-mg units, divided by 1.06), that is about 90,900 patient-years, or 9.9% of the pool. The two agree within 8%. Judgement: the Medicare treated share stands in for all payers. Younger, commercially insured patients may be more often on high-efficacy therapy, which argues for higher. Part B and D beneficiaries may overlap, and migration to Ocrevus Zunovo before 2029 would shrink the IV pool; both argue for lower. pool_crowding.py groups indications only through indication_groups, which holds no multiple sclerosis group, so on 'Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting' this asset is the only claimant and is not rationed against frexalimab ('Multiple Sclerosis') or fenebrutinib ('Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive'). That suits it: its patients are Ocrevus's, not the untreated pool's
eligible_pct.check: Value 0.09225 unchanged; note corrected. Arithmetic: lookup.py demand Ocrevus 2024 Part B 11,764 + Part D 3,085 = 14,849; 14,849/78,050 = 0.19025 (78,050 is in the frexalimab penetration source); x 0.4849 (Li, Hutton, Aparasu, as carried by the frexalimab seed) = 0.092252; x 913,925 = 84,312. Cross-check: Roche workbook US Ocrevus 2025 CHF 4,874mm x 1.215229 (book fx_rates CHF/USD 2026-09-23) = $5,923mm; CMS 2024 $668,719,044 / 11,613,701 mg = $57.58/mg, /1.06 = $54.32, x 1,200 mg = $65,185; 90,865 patient-years = 9.94% of the pool, 7.8% above 84,312. The note's claim that pool_crowding.py puts this asset in the MS group was wrong: the book's indication_groups table (and migration 065) has no MS group, group_of returns the indication's own id, and no other asset carries a penetration on id 86. Sentence rewritten.

penetration_peak_pct.unit: share of the eligible pool not yet on ABP 692, captured per year
penetration_peak_pct.source: Measured class uptake: rituximab biosimilars rose to 60% of all rituximab claims paid by Medicare Part B in 2022, four calendar years after the first US entry (Qian J, Am J Manag Care 2024;30(12):e359-e363, PMID 39745502, doi:10.37765/ajmc.2024.89644). Book path around that anchor: Part B reference claims (Rituxan + Rituxan Hycela, lookup.py demand) were 197,044 in 2020, 123,181, 91,689, 79,640 and 74,662 in 2024. Holding the total at the 229,222 that Qian's 60% implies for 2022 gives biosimilar shares of 14.0%, 46.3%, 60.0%, 65.3% and 67.4%. Amgen's slice is a third of that: 4.7%, 15.4%, 20.0%, 21.8%, 22.5%. The engine's own identity (incidence 0, 13.4% discontinuation, logistic ramp) was least-squares fitted to those five years. It gives a peak of 0.078, with RMSE 1.9 points, and an engine path of 6.8%, 13.2%, 18.1%, 21.9%, 24.6% of the pool
penetration_peak_pct.note: Judgements, three. (1) One third: three developers run comparative trials against Ocrevus. They are Amgen (NCT06700343), Sandoz (CYB704, NCT06847724; Pearce IP 2025-08-07) and Celltrion (CT-P53, Phase 3; Pearce IP 2023-05-15). Teva/Polpharma and Samsung Bioepis (added January 2026; Pearce IP 2026-01-14) are earlier, and Biocad is Russia-only. Entry order decides the slice. In rituximab, Amgen's third-to-market Riabni held about 5% of biosimilar Part B claims in 2022 (6,988 of the 137,534 implied by Qian), against 49% for Ruxience and about 46% for Truxima by residual. That is the case for lower. The case for higher is Amgen's April 2027 readout, which may put it in the first wave. (2) The class path assumes total rituximab Part B claims held flat from 2020 to 2024, and that Qian's 'all rituximab products' includes Rituxan Hycela. A subcutaneous reference that an IV biosimilar cannot replace is the Zunovo analogue. (3) After year 5 the engine keeps capturing, to a 28.9% share of the pool in year 9, above the measured plateau of 22.5%. Meanwhile the zero-incidence pool leaves out new ocrelizumab starts, so the stock falls to 25% by year 15. These two errors pull in opposite directions. Cross-check: Liu et al. (JAMA Oncol 2026, PMID 42658505) find the reference biologics' Medicare Part B market share fell 31.5% a year after biosimilar entry across bevacizumab, rituximab and trastuzumab. That is a 67.9% biosimilar share by year 3, in line with the path above
penetration_peak_pct.check: PubMed PMID 39745502 (Qian, AJMC 2024;30(12):e359-e363): biosimilars were 60% of all rituximab claims paid by Medicare Part B in 2022, four years after entry. lookup.py demand Part B reference claims (Rituxan + Rituxan Hycela): 197,044; 123,181; 91,689; 79,640; 74,662 for 2020-2024. Total 91,689/0.4 = 229,222; shares 14.0, 46.3, 60.0, 65.3, 67.4%; thirds 4.68, 15.42, 20.00, 21.75, 22.48%. Riabni 2022 6,988 claims = 5.1% of 137,534 biosimilar claims; Ruxience 67,269 = 48.9%; Truxima residual 46.0% (no Truxima row in drug_demand). Refit with the engine identity (backend/forecast.py derive_new_patients and treated_stock; pool 1, incidence 0, 13.4% discontinuation): peak 0.078, midpoint -0.35, k 5.6 gives 6.84, 13.18, 18.12, 21.87, 24.63%, RMSE 1.89 points; a grid search finds the same minimum at peak 0.078. 15-year run peaks 28.9% in year 9 and is 25.2% in year 15, as the note says. Competitors: WebSearch confirms Sandoz CYB704 (NCT06847724, Pearce IP 2025-08-07, now a comparative PK trial), Celltrion CT-P53 (NCT05906992), Teva/Polpharma licence, Samsung Bioepis adding ocrelizumab (Pearce IP 2026-01-14), Biocad Phase III. Liu (PMID 42658505) says reference share fell 31.5% a year in Part B; the note reads that as a relative decline (1 - 0.685^3 = 67.9%), one of two possible readings. The one-third share is a labelled judgement with the case both ways.

ramp_steepness.source: same least-squares fit as penetration_peak_pct: the engine's identity against Amgen's one-third slice of the rituximab biosimilar Part B share path, 2020 to 2024
ramp_steepness.note: The fit puts year-one capture at 88% of peak, so a biosimilar's uptake is close to a step. It behaves like a formulary switch at loss of exclusivity, not a brand launch. The error surface is flat along this ridge: k 9.7 with midpoint -0.2 fits the same. A ramp forced to start at half-peak (midpoint 0) needs a peak of 0.086 and fits worse (RMSE 2.3 points). The book's MS brand curve (Kesimpta, k 0.735, midpoint 3.62) would badly understate a biosimilar's first three years
ramp_steepness.check: Same refit: k 5.6 with midpoint -0.35 gives RMSE 1.89 points; k 9.7 with midpoint -0.2 gives the same 1.89 (flat ridge, as stated). Year-one capture 1/(1+exp(-5.6 x 0.35)) = 87.7% of peak. Midpoint forced to 0: best peak 0.086 at RMSE 2.33 points, as stated. Kesimpta curve k 0.735, midpoint 3.62 confirmed in the frexalimab seed.

ramp_midpoint_year.note: Negative because the measured uptake is already near its peak rate in the first full year: Truxima entered in November 2019 and the path starts in 2020. The engine takes a midpoint of 100 or below as an offset, so a negative value is valid
ramp_midpoint_year.check: Same refit as ramp_steepness. backend/forecast.py: 'mid = midpoint - years[0] if midpoint > 100 else midpoint', so -0.35 is taken as an offset and a negative value is valid.
